Flooding Disrupts Zimbabwe Transportation Equipment Industry Operations

Major flooding in the Mashonaland West Province is disrupting operations for Zimbabwe’s Transportation Equipment industry, inundating several key manufacturing and assembly sites since heavy rains began late last week. Industry executives report that water levels remain high around plants in the Chinhoyi and Banket areas, threatening the safety of facilities and forcing partial shutdowns.

Floodwaters breached the perimeter of the Nyaradzo Rolling Stock Works yesterday, halting production at its main carriage assembly hall. “We have to prioritize employee safety,” said Mavis Dube, plant manager. “All shifts have been suspended until we can assess the structural impact and ensure conditions are safe for our teams.” At least 300 workers have been sent home as the company works to pump out water and evaluate electrical systems.

According to the Zimbabwe Transportation Equipment Manufacturers Association, four other member facilities in the region are experiencing significant flooding, with assembly lines and component storage areas under water. “The risk to expensive tooling and precision machinery is severe,” said Association president Tinashe Chigova. “Many of these plants are not equipped for this level of sustained rainfall.”

Analysts estimate that as much as 60 percent of Zimbabwe’s domestic transport equipment production capacity is currently offline or operating at minimal levels. This includes manufacturers of rail wagons, bus chassis, and heavy trailer components, who rely on uninterrupted plant operations to fulfill both domestic and export contracts. “If the rains persist, we could see delays extending well into the next quarter,” said industry analyst Rufaro Moyo. “Recovery will depend on the speed of cleanup and the extent of damage to critical equipment.”

Employees at affected sites have expressed concern about job security and wages. “We understand the company’s decision, but it’s worrying for our families,” said John Murehwa, who has worked at the Chinhoyi plant for seven years. Unions are in contact with management to ensure workers receive pay during the shutdown, at least in the short term.

As of Tuesday afternoon, meteorologists are forecasting continued rain for the next 48 hours. Industry leaders are monitoring river levels and have instituted emergency protocols, including sandbagging and the relocation of high-value parts and inventory to elevated storage. The Association said they are coordinating with local authorities to expedite water removal and will conduct safety inspections at all affected sites as soon as conditions allow.

The full extent of damage and the timeline for resuming normal operations remain uncertain as the flooding continues.
